Reassessment incorporating SLOOS (April 2020) and FSR insights:
- Credit supply tightened materially. The April 2020 Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey reports widespread tightening across C&I and CRE (nonfarm nonresidential, multifamily, construction and land development), as well as HELOCs. Banks widened loan-rate spreads and premiums, raised debt-service-coverage requirements, and lowered LTVs. Reasons cited include the deteriorating economic outlook, COVID-19, industry-specific problems, liquidity needs, reduced risk tolerance, and supervisory/accounting considerations.
- Demand weakened in key sectors. Banks reported weaker demand for CRE (including construction and land development) and several industries, with some offset from stronger demand for government-backed residential mortgages and increased borrower inquiries. Many banks expected further tightening for C&I loans and were less focused on new clients, pointing to a cautious intermediation stance.
- Market functioning vs. bank intermediation. Consistent with the FSR and the FOMC statement, policy backstops (ZLB, sustained Treasury/agency MBS/CMBS purchases, robust repo/ON RRP, and credit facilities) improved market functioning and funding conditions. However, SLOOS indicates that bank lending standards remained tight, which could impede transmission to households and small and mid-sized firms despite better market liquidity.
- Implications for the statement’s tone. The SLOOS evidence of tighter standards and weaker demand reinforces a negative near-term outlook and elevates medium-term risks, outweighing—but not nullifying—the positives from improved market functioning and policy support.

Net effect: Relative to the FSR-only read, the SLOOS tilts the assessment more negative due to constrained bank credit supply and expected further tightening.
